## TL;DR (for a layperson)

Two organisations that link their networks each trust the other's certificate authority, the
"CA" that vouches for its machines. Today each side trusts exactly one CA of the other's, so
when one side replaces its CA the link stops until the other side catches up. With this
decision, a side that is about to replace its CA first tells its partner the new one, and the
two operators confirm it on a call as they already confirm the first one. For a while the
partner trusts both, the side switches its machines over, and then the old one is dropped, so
data keeps arriving throughout. The announcement goes into the next version of the package
format, because version 1 is frozen and a partner on version 1 must be refused clearly rather
than silently cut off. A CA that may have been stolen is never kept on during such a period: it
is dropped at once, and the link pauses until both sides have moved.

## Context

The package specification binds two values per party over an authenticated channel: the
signing key and `identity.ca_fingerprint` (`federation-package-spec.md` §5.1). The agreement
copies that one fingerprint into each party (§8.1), and every check that uses it accepts
exactly one CA: phase 5 confirms one fingerprint (`crates/goatbuilder/src/federate/confirm.rs`),
admission requires `partner-ca.pem` to hold exactly one certificate
(`crates/goatbuilder/src/federate/admit.rs`, "must hold exactly one certificate"), and the
edge role checks the same ([`federation-certificate-lifecycle.md`](../design/federation-certificate-lifecycle.md),
"the partner CA file holds exactly one certificate").

Rotating our CA (key K2 in [`federation-key-rotation.md`](../design/federation-key-rotation.md)
§2) therefore cannot keep data flowing: the moment our leaves are issued under the new CA, the
partner's edge refuses them, and the moment the partner trusts only the new CA, our old leaves
fail. Gate row B3 of the goatbuilder 1.0 gate requires a scenario that rotates each key in turn
while data keeps arriving ([`goatbuilder-v1-gate.md`](../design/goatbuilder-v1-gate.md)). The
key-rotation design §4 sets out an announce, switch and retire overlap and says it needs an ADR
that supersedes §5.1, and that the ADR must settle version skew, the normal case between two
sovereigns.

Two facts constrain the answer. Version 1 is pinned literally: composition refuses any package
whose `spec` is not exactly `federation-package/v1` (§6 step 1), "the format does not move"
within a version (§3.3), and the conformance vectors are normative and written by hand from the
text (§10), so a partner can implement v1 from the document alone. Second, our site roots are
made with a path length of zero (`ops/enrollment/x509ca/root.go:89`), so no intermediate CA can
sit under one, and cross-signing a new CA with the old root does not validate.

## Decision

1. **A party's CA binding is one or two fingerprints.** It is the CA that issues the party's
   leaves now and, only during a planned rotation, the CA that will issue them next. Each is a
   §5.1 value: confirmed over a channel authenticated independently of the relationship, read
   aloud by the same rule (sixteen groups of four hex characters, then read back), and recorded
   in the party's corroboration record (ADR 1170 decision 1). A next CA learned from a package,
   a directory or a SPIRE bundle without that confirmation is not bound.

2. **The next CA is a separate member.** `identity.ca_fingerprint` keeps its v1 meaning and
   format: the CA issuing the party's leaves now. A new optional member,
   `identity.ca_fingerprint_next`, has the same format (`sha256:` and 64 lowercase hex
   characters). When present it must differ from `ca_fingerprint`; an equal value is a malformed
   package, not a rotation. The agreement copies it verbatim into that party as
   `parties[n].ca_fingerprint_next` when present, and leaves the member out otherwise (never
   null, never empty, §4). Because it is in the agreement, it is in the digest: two sides whose
   digests match trust the same set.

3. **It is not added to v1.** v1's grammar, agreement and vectors stay as they are. The member
   belongs to the next version of the lineage, `federation-package/v2` and
   `federation-agreement/v2`. ADR 1230 proposes that same v2 for the listener fields; the
   lineage gets one new version carrying both, not two. This member depends on none of ADR
   1230's other decisions: if ADR 1230 is withdrawn, v2 is defined with this member alone; if it
   is accepted first, this member joins its v2 grammar before any release emits v2. Once a
   release has emitted v2, a change to it needs v3.

4. **Every check accepts exactly the set the confirmed agreement names for that party.** Phase
   5 shows each fingerprint of the partner's set and confirms each (`--partner-ca-fingerprint`
   takes one value per fingerprint, and each must match). Admission and the edge role require
   `partner-ca.pem` to hold one certificate per fingerprint in the partner's set, each a CA, no
   more and no fewer; order in the file does not matter. Our edge's `our-ca.pem` follows our own
   set the same way. A set that differs from the agreement is refused, as one fingerprint is
   refused today.

5. **A planned rotation is three runs of the command, each ending with phase 14.**
   - **Announce.** Our package carries the new CA as `ca_fingerprint_next`. It is a new package
     and a new agreement, so confirmation 1 (with ADR 1229 for the partner's side) and the
     agreement digest comparison happen again. Both sides then place both of our CAs. Our leaves
     are unchanged, so data keeps flowing.
   - **Switch.** Refused unless the agreement both sides confirmed names our new CA as
     `ca_fingerprint_next`. Phase 8 re-issues our leaves under the new CA, and phases 10 and 12
     install them. The agreement does not change. The only interruption is the edge and
     republisher restart, as for a leaf rotation (key-rotation design §3, K3).
   - **Retire.** Refused until every leaf our hosts present for this peering is issued by the
     new CA. Our package carries the new CA as `ca_fingerprint` and no `ca_fingerprint_next`. A
     new agreement is confirmed, and each side removes the old CA. Every leaf of the old CA
     stops being accepted at that moment.

   The overlap needs no timer of its own: the old CA is trusted no later than the agreement's
   `expires`, and a renewal composed while a next CA is announced carries the announcement on.

6. **Version skew is refused by name, never absorbed.** A partner that reads only v1 cannot
   compose a v2 package: §6 step 1 refuses it as a wrong `spec`. The overlap is therefore
   available only on a peering where both parties have selected v2 in reviewed configuration
   (ADR 1230 decision 3). On a v1 peering, a CA rotation is a **gap rotation**: one new agreement
   names only the new CA, both sides confirm it, and data stops from whichever side moves first
   until the other has moved. The command names that gap before it re-issues anything and does
   not start until the partner has confirmed the new agreement.

7. **A CA that may be compromised is never overlapped.** Announcing it as still trusted is what
   an attacker holding its key would want. Its retirement is a gap rotation on either version,
   started at once, and the announce step refuses when the operator records the rotation as a
   compromise.

8. **Scope is the federation follow-through.** Making a new site CA and moving every other
   service under it is the site's larger ceremony ([`internal-tls-ca.md`](../design/internal-tls-ca.md));
   this decision starts after the new CA exists. It does not cover the IPsec transport's CA,
   which is per peering and already rotates with an announce and retire of its own
   (key-rotation design §8.3), nor SPIRE's CA, which rotates itself.

9. **What is built, where.** `goat-federation` parses, composes and lints v2 with this member,
   and the v2 conformance vectors include a pair with `ca_fingerprint_next` on one side, a pair
   with it on both, and a malformed package whose next equals its current CA, written by hand
   from the specification as v1's were. `goatbuilder federate` carries the set through
   confirmation, admission and the edge role, and gains the `rotate … ca` stage the key-rotation
   design §5 describes. `federation-package-spec.md` gains the v2 text when this is built, not
   before; v1's text is unchanged.

## Alternatives considered

**Add `ca_fingerprint_next` to v1 as an optional member.** It would arrive sooner, and an older
goatcore that ignores the member would still verify the package. Rejected: v1 is literally
pinned and frozen, and its vectors are normative. A partner that implemented v1 from the
current text would compose a different agreement whenever a next CA is announced, or refuse the
package as malformed if its grammar is closed; either way the disagreement would surface as a
digest mismatch with no named cause. A version change surfaces it as a named refusal at step 1.

**Cross-sign the new CA with the old root.** No format change and one fingerprint throughout:
the partner keeps trusting the old root, and the new leaves chain to it through the cross
certificate until the agreement switches. Rejected: our roots carry a path length of zero
(`ops/enrollment/x509ca/root.go:89`), which forbids the intermediate this needs, and lifting
that means a new root, the very thing being rotated. It would also require every partner
implementation to build chains through an intermediate the specification never mentions.

**One member holding a set of one or two fingerprints.** More general, with no distinction
between the two. Rejected: the switch and retire steps need to know which CA issues leaves now
and which is next, and a set cannot say. Keeping `ca_fingerprint` with its v1 meaning also lets
one code path read the current CA from either version.

**Gap rotation only.** Works today on v1 with no format change: `--partner-ca-fingerprint`
already re-runs phase 5 onward. Kept as the path for v1 peerings and for a compromised CA.
Rejected as the only path because gate row B3 requires data to keep arriving through every
rotation.

**Learn the next CA from the partner's SPIRE bundle or a directory.** No call needed. Rejected:
§5.1 makes a directory a cache of the binding, never its source, and the peering's TLS trust is
not SPIRE's trust domain. A CA trusted without the call is a CA trusted on the word of whoever
served it.

## Consequences

**Positive.** A planned CA rotation keeps data arriving, with the same two confirmations ADR 1225
fixes and no new kind of human decision. Version skew is refused by a rule a partner can read in
the specification, not discovered as an unexplained digest mismatch. The current-CA member and
its checks are unchanged in meaning, so v1 peerings keep working as they are.

**Negative.** The CA part of gate row B3 cannot be built until v2 is: on v1 peerings only the gap
rotation exists, so row B3 cannot fully pass before both v2 and this member are built. A planned
rotation is three runs and two calls with the partner. During the overlap the old CA is still
trusted for the peering, for up to the agreement's term if a rotation is announced and left
unfinished. If ADR 1230's v2 is delayed or narrowed, this member's arrival follows it, or v2 is
defined for this member alone (decision 3).

## Assessor view (SCA-R)

The decision keeps the trust anchors for a partner's peering certificates under the same
out-of-band confirmation as the first binding, which maps to SC-12 (cryptographic key
establishment and management), SC-17 (public key infrastructure certificates), IA-5(2)
(public-key-based authentication) and IA-3 (device identification and authentication). Every
added anchor is confirmed on a call, recorded in the party's corroboration record and bound to a
compared agreement digest, which supports AU-10 (non-repudiation). Residual risk: during an
announced overlap the outgoing CA remains trusted for the peering; the compensating controls are
the bound of the agreement's `expires`, the retire step's check that no leaf of the old CA is
still presented, and the rule that a possibly compromised CA is retired at once and never
overlapped. No waiver is needed.

## Trigger conditions for revisit

- ADR 1230 is withdrawn, or a release emits v2 before this member is in its grammar: decision 3
  then takes the other branch, or the member moves to v3.
- Site roots are regenerated with a path length of one or more: cross-signing becomes possible
  and may make a format change unnecessary for later rotations.
- A partner or coalition asks to announce more than one next CA at a time.
- The site CA rotation ceremony in `internal-tls-ca.md` is built and changes when a new CA exists
  relative to the announce step.

To contribute, open a pull request against `main`. [How the two fit together](docs/design/community-and-stable-line.md). ## What goat is goat connects people, machines and services across sites into one network, and lets them publish and subscribe to data with access decided by who they are, not where they sit. The public internet sees DNS records, not open ports. - **Joined devices keep working when the centre goes down.** The management service is needed to enrol a device, not to keep it connected. # ops/gym — goat gym

The training surface. Design: [`docs/design/goat-gym.md`](../../docs/design/goat-gym.md)
([ADR 1132](https://github.com/usareur-af/goatcore/blob/main/docs/adr/1132-goat-gym-training-surface.md)). Deploy runbook:
[`docs/operations/gym-deploy.md`](../../docs/operations/gym-deploy.md).

```
gym.yaml      the registry — SINGLE SOURCE OF TRUTH (lanes, modules, drills, quirks)
content/      prose for the few modules nothing else covers
check.py      the gate + the coverage report; needs the full doc tree and goatnet declarations, so it is not a check in this repository
generate.py   renders the static site + gym.json
site/         render output — gitignored, produced at deploy time
```

```bash
python3 ops/gym/generate.py     # renders into ops/gym/site/
```

## The learning program's decision record

The shape of the learner ladder and the lane beyond it, what each mark means, and how anyone
changes the program are decided in [ADR 1238](https://github.com/usareur-af/goatcore/blob/main/docs/adr/1238-the-learning-program-is-a-ten-rung-ladder-and-a-lane-beyond-it-in-use-while-proposed.md).
It is Proposed and in use: the program is the maintainers' best guess, and the reports of the
people who learn with it decide what it becomes.

## Planned and frontier modules

A module with `status: planned` has no page. Its lane lists it as a named gap. Add
`frontier: true` to a planned module when the tooling it would teach is not built yet:
the lane then marks it "frontier" and says so, so a reader can tell a lesson that is
only unwritten from one whose subject does not exist yet. `check.py` refuses `frontier`
on a written module.

## Lane headings and the next lane

A lane may carry `headings:`, a map from a module id in the lane to a heading shown before
it, and `next:`, the id of the lane to go on to. The learner ladder is kept to its ten rungs
and points at "Beyond the ladder" this way, so a newcomer sees the ladder and not a longer list.

## Adding a module

**Point first.** If any doc in the tree explains the thing, the module is a
pointer and carries no prose of its own:

```yaml
  - id: your-module
    title: What the reader will be able to do
    level: basics | working | mastery
    minutes: 20
    mode: reference
    source:
      - path: docs/design/the-doc-that-owns-it.md
        section: §"the part that matters"      # optional
        gives: One line — what the reader gets there.
    surface: [isitup-service-id]                # optional, drives coverage
    quirks:
      - claim: >-
          The behaviour that is true and invisible on first look.
        evidence: F-123 | docs/adr/1129-….md | ops/warrant/generate.py
    drill:
      do: One command, or one thing to find.
      pass: What you should see. Not "you understand it".
      safety: read-only | writes | admin
      needs: mesh                               # optional
```

Then add the id to at least one lane's `modules:` list, in the order someone
should walk it.

**Write in place only when nothing owns it** — and say so. `no_sot:` is a
falsifiable claim, so name what you searched:

```yaml
    mode: in-place
    no_sot: >-
      Nothing documents X. Searched: docs/design/*x*, docs/operations/*x*, CLAUDE.md.
    content: ops/gym/content/your-module.md
```

If a reviewer knows the doc exists, the module is wrong and becomes a pointer.

## Rules the gate enforces, and why

- **A `source:` path must exist.** A renamed doc turns a curated pointer into a
  dead end.
- **A quirk must carry evidence.** Folklore accumulating in a surface people
  trust is worse than no surface.
- **Every module needs a drill with a pass condition.** An exercise with no pass
  condition is a suggestion.
- **`quirks: []` is required when there are none.** Silence and "none recorded"
  are different statements, and only one of them is honest.
- **A `surface:` id must be declared by some goatnet.** A typo drops the module
  out of the coverage denominator silently.

Coverage is printed, not enforced. `--strict-coverage` fails on any live isitup
service with no module, for the day the repo decides to hold that line.

## The approach in one paragraph

goat already ships by releases and tags. This design makes that pattern
consistent, so that `main` keeps moving fast and everyone knows which
version to build on and what will not change under them. The maintainers also aim
to answer validated outside contributors within one working day.

## Three names, three uses

| Name | What it is | Use it when |
|---|---|---|
| `main` | The one development branch. Every change lands here, many times a day | You are contributing. Open your pull request against `main` |
| `goatcore/vX.Y.Z` | A release of the whole repository: a signed tag at the commit of the goatbuilder release with the same version, cut after that commit has run in a standing environment | You want a fixed reference. Pin this tag |
| `stable` | A branch that always points at the newest `goatcore/v` tag. It takes no pull requests | You want the newest release by a name that does not change |

The component tags (`goatbuilder/vX.Y.Z`, `goat-cli-vX.Y.Z` and the others)
stay as they are: each publishes one component's binaries. The whole-tree
release is cut at a goatbuilder minor release, so the two share a commit and
a version.

## How the stable line moves

1. A goatbuilder minor release `X.Y.0` is tagged from `main` and published.
2. The maintainers run it in a standing environment.
3. A maintainer cuts the signed tag `goatcore/vX.Y.0` at the same commit.
4. `.github/workflows/stable.yml` runs `ops/release/stable.py check`. The
   check refuses the tag unless it names a commit on `main`, a tag
   `goatbuilder/vX.Y.0` names the same commit, and `stable` is an ancestor
   of it.
5. The workflow fast-forwards `stable` to that commit and publishes the
   release page.

Nothing else moves `stable`. `.github/workflows/stable-guard.yml` closes a
pull request opened against it and fails when a person pushes a commit that
is not a whole-tree release. A ruleset refuses deleting the branch and
moving it backwards.

A patch release moves the stable line only when a maintainer cuts
`goatcore/vX.Y.Z` for it, which they do when the patch carries a fix that
people on the stable line need.

## Which versions go together

The release page of each `goatcore/v` tag lists the newest release of each
component contained in that commit, written by
`ops/release/stable.py table`, and the versions of other projects the
release works with, kept in `ops/release/works-with.md`.

## What stays compatible

From goatbuilder 1.0, its configuration, commands and flags, machine-readable
documents and error codes change only by additions. A command, flag or field
that is to be removed keeps working, with a warning that names its
replacement, for at least two minor releases and at least 90 days, and is
removed only in the next major release ([ADR 1228](../adr/1228-goatbuilder-keeps-its-four-surfaces-and-removes-only-in-a-major-release.md)).
Before 1.0, a minor release may change an interface, and the release notes
say so. `docs/RELEASE-CONTENTS.md` lists each component and its status.

## What an outside contributor can expect

| What to expect | How it is kept |
|---|---|
| Once validated, a first reply within one working day, as an aim and not a guarantee | A contributor is validated when registered in a goat community environment with a linked GitHub account, or with an earlier merged pull request (the tier `known` of `contributor-trust`). Validation takes work from both sides and has no fixed time. The reply is in words: who has it, and what happens next |
| Outside pull requests are worked first | The `contributor-trust` check labels them `community`; maintainers work that list before their own |
| Maintainers carry the rebase | A pull request does not have to be up to date with `main` to merge. When it conflicts, a maintainer rebases it |
| Work is not replaced without a word | A maintainer's pull request that carries the same change says so in the contributor's pull request before that one is closed, and credits the commits |

A pull request from an author who is not yet known to the project also
needs a recorded security review before it merges
([CONTRIBUTING.md](../../CONTRIBUTING.md), "Outside contributions").

## Large programs

A program of many pull requests is built on a branch `integration/<name>`
and reaches `main` as a small number of reviewed changes. A program whose
releases are tagged from `main` every few days stays on `main`.

## Fixing a released version

Fixes land on `main` and are released by tag. A branch `release/X.Y` is
created from a tag only when a supported release needs a fix that cannot
wait for the next release; the fix merges to `main` first and is
cherry-picked to the branch.

## The changelog, one file per entry

goatbuilder's changelog, `crates/goatbuilder/CHANGELOG.md`, is built from
one file per entry, so a pull request that adds an entry edits no shared file
and two such pull requests never conflict. Until 19 Nov 2026 every such pull
request also committed the render of the entries into `CHANGELOG.md`'s
Unreleased section, and each merge then made every other open pull request
with an entry conflict there (nine at once). That section is now one fixed
line, never a render (built).

**Where entries live.** Each entry is a file
`crates/goatbuilder/changelog.d/<slug>.md`, its name in lower case letters,
digits and hyphens. The directory's `README.md` tells a contributor how to
write one and is not an entry.

**What an entry declares.** A header between two `---` lines, then the body:

- `heading`: one of the three headings every release uses, "For someone
  deploying", "For someone contributing" or "To be removed";
- `title`: the entry's one-line heading, for example "Fixed: a federate run
  killed in phase 11 resumes and brings the link up";
- either value may be wrapped in one matching pair of quotes, as YAML
  allows; the pair is removed before the value is checked or rendered
  (built), so a quoted title never renders with its quotes;
- the body, in Markdown, with no heading of level 1 to 3, ending with the
  pull request's number.

**The Unreleased section.** Between two marker lines under `## Unreleased`,
`CHANGELOG.md` holds one fixed line (`POINTER` in `ops/release/changelog.py`)
saying where the entries are and how to read them. Nothing reads a rendered
Unreleased section: the release folds from the entry files, the release body
is `.github/release-notes/`, and neither the book nor the compatibility
tooling reads the changelog. `ops/release/changelog.py show` prints the
entries as the next release will render them: each heading that has an
entry, as `###`, and under it each entry's title, as `####`, then its body,
in file-name order. A heading with no entry is left out. The `docs-guards`
run writes `show` into its summary. `write` puts the pointer line back.

**The check.** `ops/release/changelog.py check` fails when an entry is
malformed, when the text between the markers is anything but the pointer
line (a committed render or a hand edit; the reason says to keep the entry
and take the base branch's `CHANGELOG.md`), or
when there is text between `## Unreleased` and the first marker or between
the last marker and the newest release. It also fails when an entry's whole
rendered block (its title line, a blank line and its body; a title alone can
repeat between releases, and a title is matched quoted or unquoted, as older
sections wrote it quoted) is inside a released section. When that section at
its release does not hold the block, the entry landed there after the
release, and the check says to restore the section and keep the entry; when
it does, the entry was released and its file was left behind, and the check
says to remove the file. These reasons come before the pointer-line one. It runs in the
`docs-guards` workflow, with the whole history checked out, after its own
self-test (`--self-test`), which proves each refusal and the release step on
a copy and on a git history of its own.

**A release.** The version pull request runs `ops/release/changelog.py
release <version> <date>`. It writes `## <version> — <date>` above the
newest release, with all three headings, and "Nothing." under a heading with
no entry; it removes the entry files and leaves the pointer line. The
release's opening summary, and any grouping such as "Not in <version>", are
then added by hand in the same pull request. A released section is never
rendered again, and is never edited after its release: the check holds it to
its text at the tag `goatbuilder/v<version>`, or, before the tag exists, at
the release commit as it was committed (the oldest `chore(release):
goatbuilder <version>` commit on the first-parent history that does not touch
the baseline file below, so a release-notes change with the same subject is
never taken for it), never to a re-render. A release-notes change, the one route for editing a released
section, adds or updates that section's line in
`ops/release/changelog-released-baseline.txt` (`<version> sha256:<hash of
the section>`) in the same change. A line for a section that is as released
is refused as stale, so the list only shrinks; it starts with 0.5.3 and
0.6.0, both edited after their release. A version whose release cannot be
read (no tag and no release commit, or cut off in a shallow clone) is skipped
with a note, never passed silently.

The phase catalog's tables are rendered differently: one source, a generated
region between marker lines, a check that the region equals the render, and
`--write` to rewrite it (`ops/ci/check-phase-catalog.py`).

**A pull request cut before a release.** Built
(`ops/ci/check-changelog-base-current.py`, tests
`ops/ci/test_check_changelog_base_current.py`, in `docs-guards`). A pull
request that only adds or changes entry files merges correctly at any base. A
release made after the branch was cut did not know its file, which stays and
goes into the next release, and nothing of the entry is in `CHANGELOG.md` to
mix into the release. A test proves this on a git history of its own: an
entry-only branch cut before a release, merged after it with `git merge-tree`,
passes this check, and the merged tree alone passes `changelog.py check`, the
two steps a merge queue's changelog guard runs. A pull request that changes
`CHANGELOG.md` itself (a release, or release notes) is refused while the
base's `CHANGELOG.md` has a `## X.Y.Z` section its own lacks: it is rebased
first. Before the pointer line, a branch cut before a release carried its
rendered entry into the old Unreleased section, and a three-way merge put
those lines inside the release, as two pull requests did after 0.7.0; that
is why the check exists. The check reads the merge
GitHub made (its first parent is the base, its second the pull request's
head) with the whole history checked out. Without a merge base it fails and
says why. It cannot see a release that lands after its run; a merge made
then is refused on `main` by `changelog.py check`, which names an entry
already in a released section.

## The ADR index, one row per ADR file

`docs/adr/INDEX.md` lists every ADR. A new ADR's row is rendered from the ADR
file itself, so a pull request that adds an ADR edits no shared file.

**What an ADR declares.** Everything its row needs is already in the ADR, in
the header that `docs/adr/TEMPLATE.md` gives it:

- the number, from the file name `NNNN-<slug>.md`, one file per number;
- the title, from the first line, `# ADR NNNN — <title>`;
- the status, the `| Status | ... |` row of the header table, verbatim;
- the notes, the ADR numbers named in its `| Amends | ... |` and
  `| Supersedes | ... |` rows, written `Amends 1225; supersedes 1100`, or `—`.

A Status written another way, as a `**Status:**` line or in YAML front
matter, is refused with the reason, never read by guessing.

**Where the rows go.** The rows of ADR 1234 and below stay as they are, kept
by hand. Every ADR above 1234 is listed in one table, under the heading "ADRs
above 1234, rendered from their own files", between two marker lines. Its
columns are #, Title, Status and Notes. It is its own table because a marker
line inside a Markdown table would end the table.

**The check.** `ops/release/adr_index.py check` fails when an ADR above 1234
cannot be read, when the table differs from its render, or when a row for an
ADR above 1234 is written by hand anywhere else in the file. `write`
rewrites the table. Both run in `docs-guards`, after the script's own
self-test. The existing ADR checks stay: number uniqueness, every ADR has a
row, and an INDEX status that agrees with its ADR. A rendered row has the
same shape as a hand-kept one, so each reads both.

**Why the rows of 1234 and below are not rendered.** Rendered from their
files today, about 200 of the 359 rows would change: 62 titles differ from
the files' first lines; 203 status cells differ from the files' Status
(formatting, dates, and amendment notes kept only in INDEX), and 107 files
write their Status in another form; the fourth column holds scope, notes or
a paragraph of decision text. Thirteen rows disagree with their ADR on the
status itself, and which side is right is each owner's decision
(`ops/ci/check-adr-index-status-agrees.sh`). Moving those rows into the
render is per-owner work, one ADR at a time, after which the frozen
boundary can move down.

**What still edits a hand-kept row.** When a new ADR supersedes one of
1234 or below, the old ADR's `Superseded by` and Status change in its own
file, and its hand-kept row's Status changes to match, as before; the
status check holds the two to each other. An amendment changes nothing in
the old row: the new ADR's row says what it amends.

## `goat federate`

Federate with a partner: our half, their half, the agreement, and the configuration it implies (docs/design/federation-package-spec.md).

Two parties each publish one signed package, both compose the pair independently, and both compare the resulting digest. Equal digests prove both sides hold the identical agreement — and that comparison may travel by any channel at all, because altering a digest in transit causes a visible mismatch and causing a false match would mean forging a signature.

`lint`, `compose` and `diff` are pure: they read the files you name and nothing else, hold no credential and open no socket, so a partner can trust that handing you their package cannot touch anything. `apply` is the only verb that writes.

When two digests disagree, the verb you want is `diff`.

**Subcommands**

- [`goat federate init`](#goat-federate-init) — Generate our half of a federation, read from the running system
- [`goat federate lint`](#goat-federate-lint) — Check one package: is it well-formed, and does it agree with itself?
- [`goat federate compose`](#goat-federate-compose) — Combine two packages into one agreement and print its digest
- [`goat federate diff`](#goat-federate-diff) — Two digests disagree? Run this. It names the field
- [`goat federate verify`](#goat-federate-verify) — Could we actually deliver this agreement? Dry-run it here
- [`goat federate apply`](#goat-federate-apply) — Render the access rules and configuration this agreement implies

## `goat federate init`

Generate our half of a federation, read from the running system.

Every capability in the package is MEASURED here, not typed: what transports are installed and configured, what image the router is actually running, what version the fabric is. A capability an operator types is a claim, and a wrong claim stays wrong until the link fails in front of a partner.

Where a value cannot be derived this fails and names it. It never prompts and never fills one in — a silent default is how a link ends up with no rate limit.

Exit 23 means something could not be derived; the list is the output.

|---|---|---|

## `goat federate compose`

Combine two packages into one agreement and print its digest.

Both parties compose independently and compare the digest. Equal digests prove both sides hold the identical agreement — that is the whole point of the format, and the comparison may travel by any channel at all, including one nobody trusts.

A refusal is an outcome, not a failure: it is the mechanism working. Exit 20, with the rule that fired.

Reads two files and the keys you pass. No network, no credentials, no host access — this runs in an empty container, which is what lets a partner trust it with their package.

**Arguments**

| Argument | Description |
|---|---|
| `<FIRST>` | One party's package |
| `<SECOND>` | The other party's package. Order does not matter: the agreement has no "us" and "them", so both sides compute the same bytes whichever way round they pass the files |

| Flag | Description | Default |
|---|---|---|

## `goat access key rotate`

Rotate this member's grant-encryption LEAF KEY — the key used to unwrap the DEKs that open sealed streams (`goat sub --open`). A convenience over the grant-crypto SDK's `rotate` (ADR 1106); it computes the rotation locally (the platform holds no keys and never re-wraps) and prints a structured RotationReceipt.

Two policies: `--destroy` (DEFAULT) drops the retiring key and re-wraps nothing — full forward secrecy for pre-rotation generations; `--keep-access` re-wraps this member's still-live DEKs to the new key, which REDUCES forward secrecy for those generations.

This is DISTINCT from `goat admin rotate` (org cert reissue). Because a member's grant-encryption leaf key IS its mTLS profile key — whose re-issue is a CA operation (ADR 1044) — this verb NEVER overwrites your profile: it writes the freshly generated key to `--out` for you to install via the CA-coupled leaf re-issue so your cert continues to match. ## `goat audit emit`

Emit ONE operator-action record on behalf of another surface.

This exists because the on-wire record is `age(protobuf(OperatorActionV1))` and this crate holds the only implementation of that encoding — the proto warns that any change must be mirrored field-for-field, tag-for-tag, or the wire breaks silently. A surface written in another language (herd, ADR 1131) would otherwise need a second copy of the format to be auditable at all, and two copies of a wire format is how one of them drifts.

`--actor` is the PERSON the action belongs to, NOT whoever runs this command. That is the whole point: a forwarder emitting herd's records must attribute them to the person who opened the session, or attribution collapses onto the forwarder and the audit answers nothing.

SAID PLAINLY: emitting on behalf of another surface is a TRUSTED operation. Anyone able to run this already holds a roster identity, and nothing here proves the named actor really did the thing. What the record does carry is `surface`, `host` and `src` — so a forged actor is still traceable to the box that emitted it. Do not extend this to accept a caller-supplied host or src.

| Flag | Description | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `--actor <ACTOR>` | The person this action belongs to (kebab operator handle) |  |
| `--surface <SURFACE>` | Emitting surface, e.g. `herd` |  |
| `--action <ACTION>` | Semantic verb, e.g. `gear.session.open` |  |

## `goat admin onboard`

REVOKE an operator / org by handle — the live offboarding path (ADR 1031).

The ENROLL direction is RETIRED (July 2026, ADR 1062 cutover) and refuses. It minted every surface from a hand-authored manifest and wrote an out-of-band bundle carrying the person's private key; the live path never puts a key in an operator's hands. Bring people on with `goat admin invite --env <goatnet>` and the three-stage candidate flow, then reconcile the roster with ops/scripts/sync-onboarded-manifests.py. The refusal names the override if you genuinely need it.

Two implementations underneath, both fenced for enroll and both live for revoke: a native fast path (portal + NetBird API + Ory over SSH, seconds) which is the DEFAULT when the manifest is native-serviceable, and `ops/scripts/ansible-preflight.sh operator-onboard.yml` otherwise. `--native` / `--ansible` force one. Streams child output line-by-line; SIGINT propagates via the process group (tokio::process default).

**Arguments**

| Argument | Description |
|---|---|
| `<HANDLE>` | Handle (kebab-case slug). Manifest must exist at `ops/operators/<handle>.yml` (flat / legacy) or, when `--env <env>` is passed, `ops/operators/<env>/<handle>.yml` in the discovered repo root. Omit when using `--org` |

**Options**

| Flag | Description | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `--org <ORG>` | ORG-scope revoke (cascade). Instead of one handle, revoke EVERY active member of the affiliation org `<id>` (the `affiliation.id`, e.g. `acme`) — persons + systems, the whole unit. Resolves the members from the declared registry (`docs/operators/roster.json`, the affiliation-grouped roster) and runs the per-handle revoke for each, after printing the blast radius and asking to confirm (skip the prompt with `--yes`). Requires `--revoke`; mutually exclusive with a positional handle. Identity grammar B.4 / ADR 1031 org-cascade (`docs/design/credential-revocation-and-offboarding.md`) |  |
| `--yes` | Skip the interactive confirmation prompt for `--org` cascades. For scripted/non-interactive use; the blast radius is still printed |  |
| `--env <ENV>` | Environment / goatnet the manifest belongs to (e.g. `zagros`, `zagros-prod`). Selects the per-env manifest subfolder `ops/operators/<env>/<handle>.yml` and is passed to the playbook as `-e operator_env=<env>` so the per-site maps (NetBird mgmt URL, Ory Kratos admin host, Zenoh portal) resolve to that goatnet. Required on every live goatnet: with no env the native legs resolve to no config and defer |  |
| `--revoke` | Revoke instead of enroll. Cuts every provisioned surface — NetBird peer(s), Ory login, the Zenoh slot (guarded when teammates share it) — and flips the manifest to `status: revoked`. Reversible by default (Ory deactivate, registry deprecate): a returning principal is a re-onboard, not lost. Takes the native fast path (~seconds) when the env/manifest is native-serviceable; `--ansible` forces the playbook |  |
| `--purge` | With `--revoke`: terminally DELETE the Ory identity instead of the default reversible deactivate (state=inactive). Irreversible — use for a hard offboard where the login must not be recoverable. The Zenoh slot + NetBird peer are cut either way. Mirrors the playbook's `-e revoke_purge=true` (Phase R2.3) |  |
| `--from <FROM>` | With `--revoke`: batch-revoke every handle listed in FILE (one kebab-case handle per line; `#` comments and blanks ignored). Each is revoked natively and independently — a per-handle failure is reported, never aborts the batch. The generalized cohort-revoke path (the sweep tool). Mutually exclusive with a positional handle and `--org` |  |
| `--repair` | Re-mint a partial bundle in place: run the (hardened) revoke leg then the enroll leg as one operation, so every surface is freshly minted and rendered into one complete bundle. The all-or-nothing render means a half-provisioned bundle can't be completed by a plain re-run — this is the supported repair. The revoke leg frees the surfaces but leaves the manifest `status: active` (via `-e onboard_repair=true`) so the enroll leg re-mints onto it. See P1.5 in docs/design/onboard-rotate-revoke-streamlining.md. Mutually exclusive with --revoke |  |
| `--reissue-handset-key` | Revoke every live HANDSET key this person holds on the goatnet and mint a fresh one (a lost or replaced phone, ADR 1175). Touches nothing else: the device key, the Ory login and the Zenoh slot stay as they are, and no bundle is rendered. Native only. Refuses when the manifest says `netbird.handset_limit: 0` |  |
| `--reissue-device-key` | Mint a fresh DEVICE setup key for an already-onboarded person whose key has expired or been used up, and revoke any device key of theirs that is still live, so the person holds exactly one. Touches nothing else: enrolled peers, the handset key, the Ory login and the Zenoh slot stay as they are, and no bundle is rendered. Groups and the key name come from the manifest; with no manifest on this machine they come from the person's most recent device key on the goatnet (what they were actually granted), and the command says which it used. Records an operator-action audit event naming the operator, the person and the key. Native only. Console: "Reissue device key" |  |
| `--uses <USES>` | With `--reissue-device-key`: how many enrollments the fresh key allows (1-100). Default: the manifest's `netbird.usage_limit`, else 5 |  |
| `--requested-by <REQUESTED_BY>` | With either reissue flag: who asked for the key (the console user's email when the onboard-runner runs it on their behalf). Recorded on the audit event beside the operator who ran the command |  |
| `--native` | Force the native fast path (the DEFAULT for a plain enroll — provisions all three identity surfaces directly, no Ansible, seconds not minutes; mirrors `goat admin rotate`). Mints the Zenoh wire-layer (`POST /api/orgs` → slot/cert/key), the NetBird mesh setup key, AND the Ory Kratos login identity (over an SSH shell-out to the site Thor's Kratos admin API) — P2.1/P2.2/P2.4. Native config covers zagros/zagros-prod/zagros-dev; other envs defer that leg to Ansible with a clear note. The Ory leg runs last — a failure there leaves the Zenoh/NetBird bundle usable, marked `partial`, never silently dropped. The Ory operator-IdP surface stays on Ansible. As of goat-cli 0.4.13 the native path is the DEFAULT for BOTH enroll and revoke; this flag now only FORCES it (erroring if the env/manifest isn't native-serviceable) — pass `--ansible` for the legacy playbook. Not valid with --repair (which sequences a revoke+enroll through the playbook). See docs/design/onboard-rotate-revoke-streamlining.md |  |
| `--defer-credential` | Onboard the Zenoh slot WITHOUT minting its fabric credential (mint-on-collect, docs/design/fabric-credential-collection.md). The slot, the person linkage and the org row are created; no api_key and no cert are. The person mints their own from the console's fabric-credential page once they can sign in — which is the only way the key reaches them rather than passing through an operator and an email, since the plaintext can never be shown a second time |  |
| `--ansible` | Force the legacy Ansible playbook (`operator-onboard.yml`) instead of the native fast path — for enroll OR revoke. Use it when you need a surface native doesn't do (Ory operator-IdP, an env with no native config, observer/prod Zenoh flavours) or to fall back deliberately. Repair always uses the playbook regardless |  |
| `--repo-root <REPO_ROOT>` | Override repo root (defaults to searching upward from cwd for a `.git` directory) |  |
| `--collab <COLLAB>` | With `--revoke`: record what happens to this person's CLOUD COLLABORATION account (Outline / files / chat behind Dex+Kanidm) — `keep` or `revoke`. That plane is a separate identity store the mesh revoke deliberately does not cut, so the choice is a decision this command RECORDS (receipt line + audit event), not a cut it performs: goat-cli holds no collab credentials, and minting a second client + credential path for them is exactly what the provisioner seam avoids. `--collab revoke` prints the one command that does cut it (`onboard-runner -collab revoke`). Omit the flag and the receipt says `undecided` — honest, and the reconcile will keep surfacing the person until someone chooses. Native-path only. See F-274 + docs/design/credential-revocation-and-offboarding.md |  |
| `--dry-run` | Don't actually run ansible-playbook; print the command + exit 0. Useful for previewing in CI / scripts |  |

## `goat admin rotate`

Re-issue (rotate) a peer's cert in place — same anchor, fresh leaf. The "rotate" sibling of `--revoke`: use it for expiry renewal, post-compromise rotation, or retrofitting a new URI-SAN scheme onto an already-issued cert, all WITHOUT changing the peer's anchor / alias / write namespace / ACL. Pure-portal POST /api/orgs/{anchor}/rotate, operator-gated server-side. The selector is an anchor (32-hex slot_id) or its slot alias; the alias is resolved to the anchor before the call. Prints the fresh one-time bundle URL — fetch it, swap the cert+key on the peer, and restart it. See docs/design/credential-rotation.md

**Arguments**

| Argument | Description |
|---|---|
| `<SELECTOR>` | Anchor (slot_id) or its slot alias to re-issue. Omit when using `--org` |

**Options**

| Flag | Description | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `--org <ORG>` | ORG-scope rotation (cascade). Instead of one selector, re-issue the leaf cert of EVERY active member of the affiliation org `<id>` (the `affiliation.id`) in place — the rotate sibling of the `onboard --org --revoke` cascade, at the same granularity. Resolves the members from the declared registry (`docs/operators/roster.json`) and resolves each to its slot anchor via the alias map; members with no resolvable anchor are reported and skipped (fail-visible, never silent). Prints the blast radius and asks to confirm (skip with `--yes`). Mutually exclusive with a positional selector. Identity grammar / ADR 1044 (`docs/design/credential-rotation.md`) |  |
| `--yes` | Skip the interactive confirmation prompt for `--org` cascades. The blast radius is still printed |  |
| `--repo-root <REPO_ROOT>` | Repo root holding `docs/operators/roster.json` for `--org` resolution. Defaults to the nearest `.git` ancestor of the cwd |  |
| `--dry-run` | Don't actually POST; resolve the selector(s) + print the intended request(s) + exit 0 |  |
| `--key-only` | Reissue ONLY the portal key, leaving the mTLS cert untouched (goat#1193). The lighter, safer path for the recurring case: someone lost / mistyped / stale-pasted their portal key but their cert is fine and they are still publishing. Swaps the key in place with zero cert churn — no bundle, no download, no peer restart. Without it, `rotate` re-mints the cert too. Single-anchor only, not the `--org` cascade |  |

## `goat admin peer`

Mesh-peer lifecycle — the authoritative mesh-first cut. `ls` lists mesh peers; `cut` ejects one (deletes its NetBird peer, so its WireGuard tunnel drops). On a brokerless slot-pool fabric the Zenoh write-ACL is pre-baked for the whole pool, so deleting an org record does NOT stop a flooder — removing the *peer* does (a cert is inert without a mesh path). This is the one-command emergency cut: `goat health` finds the hog, `goat admin peer cut` ejects it. Needs the NetBird admin token in the environment ($<CONTEXT>_NB_API_TOKEN, e.g. ZAGROS_NB_API_TOKEN, or $GOAT_NB_API_TOKEN)

**Subcommands**

- [`goat admin peer ls`](#goat-admin-peer-ls) — List mesh peers (id, name, mesh IP, connected, last-seen, groups). The IP shown is the mesh address (100.64.x.x on wt0) — NOT a LAN address. Direct-vs-relayed is peer-local runtime state (`netbird status` / the mesh-health domain), not in the mgmt-API peer list
- [`goat admin peer cut`](#goat-admin-peer-cut) — Eject a peer from the mesh — the authoritative cut. Selector is an exact peer id, an exact mesh IP, or a case-insensitive substring of the peer name/hostname (as shown by `ls`). Refuses if the selector matches more than one peer (re-run with a more specific selector)

## `goat admin pqc`

Toggle PQC on an ALREADY-ENROLLED peer at BOTH layers — the Zenoh kx-mode state file (F-259 Tier 1 kill-switch, `/var/lib/goat/pqc-mode`; new processes latch it, long-running surfaces flip on restart) and intra-mesh Rosenpass (ADR 0602) — no setup key, no re-mint. The rosenpass leg runs `netbird down` then `netbird up` with the explicit flag (`--enable-rosenpass --rosenpass-permissive` for `on`, `--enable-rosenpass=false` for `off`). Both the `down` and the explicit-`false` matter: a bare `up` no-ops on a connected peer AND persists the prior setting, so it silently changes nothing. The toggle briefly drops + re-establishes the tunnel. Permissive means `on` never breaks connectivity to not-yet-enabled peers, and PQC only actually engages between two Rosenpass-enabled peers — so a mixed fleet is safe.

This is the OTHER-peer surface — admin-gated (needs the NetBird API token plus SSH). To toggle THIS host, use `goat client pqc` instead (self-service, no admin token). Here you MUST pass `--peer` or `--fleet`. With `--peer <sel>` it SSHes to a mesh peer (the one-command "PQC-ify everything hosted on a mgmt-host" — e.g. Thor's own peer PQ-secures every service riding it). With `--fleet` it prints the per-peer plan for the whole mesh (each peer holds its OWN setting, so a fleet flip is a per-peer re-up, not an instant switch; the durable path is the `rosenpass_enabled` ansible group_var + re-onboard). See docs/design/rosenpass-intra-mesh-pqc.md.

**Arguments**

| Argument | Description |
|---|---|
| `<STATE>` | `on` (enable Rosenpass) or `off` (revert to classical WireGuard) |

**Options**

| Flag | Description | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `--peer <PEER>` | Toggle a remote mesh peer over SSH instead of this host. Selector is an exact peer id, exact mesh IP, or a case-insensitive name/hostname substring (as shown by `goat admin peer ls`). Refuses if it matches more than one peer. SSHes `<ssh-user>@<mesh-ip>` and runs the netbird command with `sudo` |  |
| `--fleet` | Print the per-peer plan for every mesh peer (the honest "sweep": PQC is per-peer, so this emits the command to run on each rather than fanning SSH into heterogeneous peers). Combine with `--json` for machine-readable output |  |
| `--ssh-user <SSH_USER>` | SSH user for `--peer` (default: the context's `mgmt_ssh_user`, written by `goat context refresh`) |  |
| `--mgmt-url <MGMT_URL>` | Override the NetBird mgmt URL for peer resolution (else env / profile) |  |
| `--yes, -y` | Skip the confirmation prompt (`--peer` mutates the remote mesh client) |  |
| `--dry-run` | Resolve + print what WOULD run, change nothing, exit 0 |  |
| `--json` | Emit JSON instead of the human summary |  |
